title: Introduction to OpenShift
subtitle: Deploy an app and learn the main OpenShift resources.
description: Use projects, Pods, Deployments, Services, and Routes to run an application. Prepare an arbitrary-UID-compatible image and configure JVM resource requests and limits.

lessons.title: OCP, Kubernetes & projects
lessons.summary: OpenShift builds on Kubernetes and adds developer tooling and platform controls. A project scopes access and resources.
objectives: Explain the relationship between OpenShift and Kubernetes.
Switch the active project with oc.
keyPoints: Kubernetes resources and concepts apply in OpenShift.
A project adds OpenShift access and management features to a namespace.
This module focuses on application deployment, not cluster administration.
practice: Create or select a sandbox project and inspect its resources with oc.
Commands run in the intended project with appropriate access.

exercises.prompt: Which statement best describes OpenShift and Kubernetes?
options: OpenShift is a Kubernetes-based platform with additional developer, security, and operations features.
OpenShift is an incompatible replacement for Kubernetes.
OpenShift is another name for Docker.
Kubernetes is an OpenShift plugin.
exercises.explanation: Kubernetes knowledge carries over to OpenShift, which adds resources such as Route and controls such as SCC.

exercises.prompt: Which oc command switches to project belajar-microservices?
exercises.hint: Use oc project followed by the project name.
exercises.explanation: oc project belajar-microservices changes the active project. oc projects lists projects you can access.

lessons.title: Pod, Deployment & Service
lessons.summary: Pods run containers, Deployments manage replicas and rollouts, and Services give callers a stable address.
objectives: Match a Deployment selector to pod labels.
Use a Service instead of a pod IP.
keyPoints: A pod is replaceable and may receive a new IP.
Deployment manages ReplicaSets and desired replica count.
Service selects matching ready pods behind stable DNS.
practice: Deploy two replicas and expose them through a Service on port 8080.
Replacing a pod does not require callers to discover a new pod IP.

exercises.prompt: Complete a Deployment with 2 replicas, selector and pod label app: order, and image image-registry.openshift-image-registry.svc:5000/belajar/order:0.1 on port 8080.
checks: Set pod template label app: order
exercises.explanation: The selector must match the pod template labels. The Service uses labels to select ready pods.

exercises.prompt: Why should another application call Order through a Service instead of a pod IP?
options: Pod IPs change; a Service provides stable DNS and an IP while routing to ready pods.
Pod IPs can never be accessed.
A Service automatically makes application code faster.
A Service stores application data.
exercises.explanation: Service separates callers from replaceable pod instances and routes traffic to those that are ready.

lessons.title: Route & application access
lessons.summary: A Route maps an external hostname to a Service through the OpenShift router.
objectives: Compare edge, passthrough, and re-encrypt TLS.
Trace a request from a browser to a pod.
keyPoints: Edge terminates client TLS at the router.
Passthrough sends TLS through to the pod; re-encrypt creates a second TLS connection.
A Route targets a Service, which selects application pods.
practice: Create an edge Route for the order Service.
The application is reachable through the Route’s HTTPS hostname.

exercises.prompt: With edge TLS termination, which connection is encrypted?
options: Browser to OpenShift router; router to pod uses plain HTTP.
Browser to pod with no intermediate decryption.
None.
Only router to pod.
exercises.explanation: Use re-encrypt or passthrough when the internal connection must also be encrypted.

exercises.prompt: Order a request’s path from the user to Spring Boot.
items: The OpenShift router receives the request and matches the Route.
The Route forwards to Service order.
The Service selects a ready pod.
Spring Boot processes the request on port 8080 in the pod.
exercises.explanation: Route handles external routing and TLS; Service provides stable addressing and pod selection.

lessons.title: Arbitrary UID & resource limits
lessons.summary: Prepare writable directories for OpenShift’s assigned UID and budget JVM memory within container limits.
objectives: Make required directories writable through group permissions.
keyPoints: Group-based permissions support arbitrary UIDs without running as root.
Requests guide scheduling; limits constrain resource use.
Heap is only part of JVM memory, so reserve room for non-heap usage.
practice: Run the image as a different UID locally and deploy it with explicit resources.
The app can write required files without privileged SCCs and stays within its memory budget.

exercises.prompt: Prepare /app/data for an arbitrary UID: assign group 0, give the group owner-equivalent permissions, and use USER 1001.
checks: Set the directory group to root with chgrp -R 0
exercises.explanation: Group permissions allow the assigned UID to access the required directory without relaxing SCC controls.

exercises.prompt: A pod repeatedly reports OOMKilled. What should you investigate first?
options: It exceeded its memory limit; inspect JVM heap and non-heap use and tune the limit or MaxRAMPercentage.
The disk is full; delete logs.
The image is missing; rename it.
Disable readiness probes.
exercises.explanation: JVM memory includes heap, metaspace, stacks, buffers, and code cache. Leave headroom below the container limit.

exercises.prompt: The image fails with Permission denied writing /app/data. What is the best fix?
options: Fix the directory’s group-0 ownership and group write permission in the image.
Request anyuid so it can run as root.
Request privileged SCC.
Make every file chmod 777.
exercises.explanation: Fix the image’s required directory permissions rather than broadly weakening container or cluster access controls.
